items.title: 23.9 Hydrolysis of Acyl Chlorides, Alkyl Chlorides and Aryl Chlorides

source_refs.note: Topic 23.9 with Quick Check 23.5, printed pages 111-112 (PDF 114-115). The exercises (PDF 115-117) are not part of the lesson.

blocks.text: The reactivity of acyl chlorides, alkyl chlorides and aryl (arene) chlorides can be compared with the ease of hydrolysis they undergo. Let us consider the following reactions.

blocks.alt: Three reactions with water. Ethanoyl chloride, CH3-C(=O)-Cl, + H2O, 'Room temperature, rapid', gives ethanoic acid + HCl. Chloroethane, CH3-CH2-Cl, + H2O, 'Heat under reflux', gives ethanol + HCl. Chlorobenzene + H2O gives No Reaction.
blocks.caption: Hydrolysis of ethanoyl chloride, chloroethane and chlorobenzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 114).

blocks.text: In ethanoyl chloride, the carbonyl carbon is having partial positive charge due to the strong electron withdrawing effect of two highly electronegative atoms: oxygen and chlorine directly attached to the carbon. Hence nucleophilic attack of H₂O on electrophilic carbon is so fast that reaction is completed within few minutes.

In ethyl chloride, the carbon gets comparatively less partial positive charge because it is attached to only chlorine atom. So, the nucleophilic attack of water is comparatively slow and takes 14 days to be completed even at 100°C.
book_errors: takes 14 days to be completed even at 100°C

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: No standard source gives '14 days even at 100 °C', and it does not fit the measured rate: even at 25 °C the half-life of chloroethane in water is only about six weeks, and the rate rises steeply on heating, so at 100 °C hydrolysis is complete in far less than 14 days. The book's point stands: an alkyl chloride is hydrolysed much more slowly than an acyl chloride and has to be heated under reflux.

On the other hand in chlorobenzene, the carbon bonded to chlorine is the part of benzene ring. Here, lone pair on chlorine participates in delocalization with π elections of the benzene ring. This will create a double bond character in C-Cl bond making it so strong that it will not break and, hence, does not take part in the chemical reaction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: 'π elections' is a misprint for π electrons.

blocks.prompt: a) Why do phenols not react directly with carboxylic acids to form phenyl esters?
blocks.explanation: The lone pair of the phenol oxygen is delocalised into the benzene ring, so phenol is a weak nucleophile and cannot attack the weakly electrophilic carbon of a carboxylic acid effectively. So the more reactive acyl chloride is used.

blocks.prompt: b) Phenyl ethanoate is the ester responsible for the fragrance of peach and strawberry. It can be prepared from the ethanoyl chloride and phenol. Write down a chemical reaction for the preparation of this ester.
blocks.explanation: CH₃COCl + C₆H₅OH → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl (warm gently; a base such as NaOH helps by forming the phenoxide ion).

blocks.prompt:
c) Predict the products of the following reactions, write the chemical equations.
I) Chlorobenzene and ethanol
ii) Propanoyl chloride and phenol
blocks.explanation:
I) No reaction: the C–Cl bond of chlorobenzene is very strong.
ii) CH₃CH₂COCl + C₆H₅OH → CH₃CH₂COOC₆H₅ + HCl (phenyl propanoate)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Phenyl ethanoate (phenyl acetate) is not the fragrance of peach or strawberry; it has a phenol-like smell. The fruity, jasmine-like ester used in strawberry and pear flavours is benzyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂C₆H₅, and peach aroma comes mainly from lactones such as γ-undecalactone. The preparation asked for (ethanoyl chloride + phenol) is correct.
